title: App Demo Storyboard Template: Plan the Screens Before You Edit
description: Plan a demo shot by shot with a six-frame example, a recording handoff worksheet and continuity checks.
lede: Plan a demo shot by shot with a six-frame example, a recording handoff worksheet and continuity checks.
intent: Visual shot planning; the existing script guide owns spoken copy.

sections.heading: Start with one visible answer
paragraphs: Write the viewer’s question above the storyboard. “Where is the next step from Monday’s call?” tells the recorder which screen proves the answer. “Show our productivity platform” leaves that decision unresolved.

NorthStar below is a fictional notes app, not a customer or an integration. Its project Atlas contains a Monday call note with a next-step section. Replace these labels with real controls in your product.

sections.heading: Draw the frames that carry the task
paragraphs: A box with the selected object, control and annotation is enough. Number each frame and identify its start state, the action between frames and end state. Separate the click on Call notes from the readable list that appears.

The schematic below is an original planning diagram, not an app screenshot. Expand its three major states into the six recording instructions in the table. A storyboard is useful when it resolves what to capture, rather than merely repeating narration.

sections.heading: Preserve continuity across cuts
paragraphs: Carry one recognizable object through the sequence: Atlas, Monday’s call and its next step. Switching sample projects makes an accurate demonstration hard to follow. Mark crop boundaries so the selected control and result remain connected.
When moving to a close-up, retain an orientation cue. Do not cut directly from an overview to a finished note if viewers need to learn how to open it.

sections.heading: Hand the plan to the recorder
paragraphs: Give each frame a filename and retake condition. “03-open-monday; retake if a notification covers the title” is actionable. Record with approved sample data and compare the footage with the strip before editing.

If a control is unavailable, revise storyboard and narration together. Do not manufacture a screen to preserve a sentence. Ask a fresh reviewer which note was opened and where the next step appeared; incorrect answers identify missing evidence.

title: Turn a Widescreen SaaS Demo into a Readable Vertical Video
description: Compare fit, crop and sequential close-ups with pixel arithmetic, a framing decision table and an export-review worksheet.
lede: Compare fit, crop and sequential close-ups with pixel arithmetic, a framing decision table and an export-review worksheet.
intent: Spatial reframing; separate from capture setup and the editing sequence.

sections.heading: Find the smallest useful proof region
paragraphs: Mark the control viewers must recognize and the result they must read. If they sit on opposite sides of a dashboard, one portrait crop may not contain both. In this fictional reporting-app example, select This week and read the resulting date range. Decorative charts are unnecessary evidence.
Removing clutter from composition is different from changing a product result. Preserve qualifications and validation messages that affect its meaning.

sections.heading: Calculate what a phone preview does to the source
paragraphs: Consider an illustrative 1280 × 720 recording. A 9:16 crop at full source height is 405 pixels wide. Fitting the entire width into a 360-pixel preview produces about 360 × 203 pixels. A 16-pixel source label appears about 4.5 pixels high.

These are example calculations, not upload requirements or universal readability thresholds. Use your actual source and destination preview. They explain why a technically complete desktop view can fail a phone reading test.

sections.heading: Choose fit, crop or a sequence
paragraphs: Fit the entire screen when overall arrangement matters and small labels are unimportant. Crop when action and result share a compact region. Use sequential close-ups when the workflow crosses distant regions.
Show the date selection before moving to its result. Keep an orientation cue through the move. A finished result alone does not establish which action produced it.

sections.heading: Review causality and the actual export
paragraphs: Let a selection complete before moving the frame. A sudden pan during a click can hide the chosen option. If a menu extends beyond the crop, widen it or record another pass. Enlargement cannot recover absent source detail.

Open the export at normal phone viewing size. Ask someone to name the option and changed result without zooming. Record their answer and revise the failing interval. This is a comprehension check, not evidence of improved campaign performance.

title: App Launch Video Checklist: Assets, Review and Release Readiness
description: Build a launch-video manifest covering destination, product version, eligibility, approval, fallback and link checks.
lede: Build a launch-video manifest covering destination, product version, eligibility, approval, fallback and link checks.
intent: Launch asset readiness; separate from acquisition strategy.

sections.heading: Create one manifest row per destination
paragraphs: A store listing, social post and landing-page embed can need different footage or endings. Give each row an owner, export revision and acceptance condition before editing.

This example uses a fictional habit app launching a weekly summary. Suppose iOS is ready while Android support is pending. Preserve that distinction; a development screen is not proof of universal availability.

sections.heading: Confirm the release and audience
paragraphs: Record the capture build and plans, roles, devices or regions that can access the feature. Ask the release owner to confirm rollout details. If availability is unresolved, hold the asset or obtain approval for precisely scoped wording.
Do not invent an Android interface to simplify the message. Keep a truthful fallback: an approved general demonstration, an availability page or a decision to wait.

sections.heading: Review footage, rights and destination rules
paragraphs: Check sample data, notifications, music, faces and third-party assets. Attach approval to the exact export, not a vaguely named folder. Review store destinations against their current official guidance.

Apple and Google Play publish separate preview-asset requirements. A social edit with reaction footage should not automatically become a store asset. Use the linked sources for the specific destination and file.

sections.heading: Rehearse the handoff and hosted review
paragraphs: Have someone identify approved and held rows without help. Open every next-step link in its intended device context. Confirm what an unsupported visitor encounters and who can replace an incorrect export.

This is a proposed tabletop exercise, not a tested customer launch. After release, record the date and verify hosted files separately. Local source review, creative approval and public release are distinct states.

title: SaaS Feature Announcement Video: Turn a Release Note into a Demo
description: Translate a release note into a focused demonstration with a change-to-screen matrix, rollout checks and a handoff worksheet.
lede: Translate a release note into a focused demonstration with a change-to-screen matrix, rollout checks and a handoff worksheet.
intent: Existing-user change communication, not a product introduction.

sections.heading: Translate the release note into a task
paragraphs: “Assignee filter added” describes a feature. “Find the tasks assigned to you in this project” gives an existing user an action. Write the old difficulty and new action before planning scenes.
This example uses a fictional project app with a new assignee filter. It is an editorial exercise, not evidence of a UGC Pilot feature or a customer result.

sections.heading: Prove the exact change
paragraphs: Record the list before filtering, select the current-user option and show the resulting rows. Keep the selection visible as the result changes. If the filter affects only the current project, do not describe workspace-wide search.

Check words such as all, automatic and instant against the release. A narrow statement supported by the screen is better than an expansive promise. If no honest before recording exists, demonstrate the current method without fabricating a slow old experience.

sections.heading: Make eligibility part of the message
paragraphs: Ask the release owner which plans, roles and rollout groups see the control. A signed-in user can still be ineligible. Check whether mobile or another workspace role has a different interface.

For staged availability, use an owner-confirmed statement and a relevant information path. Do not invite everyone to a control that many cannot see. A help page may be a better next step than a universal “try it now.”

sections.heading: Review versions and adoption
paragraphs: Name the export after the feature and revision. Have an eligible reviewer follow its steps. Ask an ineligible reviewer to check whether the access explanation makes sense. Record actual feedback rather than assuming comprehension.

End with the smallest useful adoption action: open the task list and choose the assignee filter. General signup messaging serves a different audience. Keep the release note and help path available for people who need detail.

title: App Store Preview vs Social Promo Video: Plan Separate Assets
description: Compare store-preview and social-video decisions with a destination matrix, shared-footage worksheet and official platform references.
lede: Compare store-preview and social-video decisions with a destination matrix, shared-footage worksheet and official platform references.
intent: Destination-specific asset selection, not a software-vendor comparison.

sections.heading: Write the question at each destination
paragraphs: Someone on a store listing may be evaluating an install. A social viewer may not yet recognize the problem. A landing-page visitor may need evidence for one feature claim. Treat these as audience hypotheses to check, not guaranteed behavior.
Write the question for each placement. This explains why the same opening, ending and footage might not suit every location, even when all versions describe the same truthful task.

sections.heading: Check current official requirements
paragraphs: Apple’s app-preview guidance emphasizes demonstrating the app experience using device-captured footage. Its specifications and submission guidance govern the file you prepare. Google Play provides separate preview-asset and video guidance.

Read the linked official pages for the destination, device and locale. A remembered export size is not a compliance check. This guide neither certifies acceptance nor uploads a store video on your behalf.

sections.heading: Share source recordings, not assumptions
paragraphs: For a fictional timer app, capture the real action of grouping work sessions and the resulting grouped view. Keep that source apart from destination exports. Reuse it only where permissions and destination rules allow.

A social version might introduce the viewer’s problem. A store version needs its own review as an app experience. A landing version could focus on the grouped result. None should add behavior the source cannot establish.

sections.heading: Version exports and recheck at upload
paragraphs: Label each export by placement and obtain separate approval. Check opening, overlays, narration, device presentation, rights and ending. When requirements conflict, make separate assets or hold the destination rather than dropping a necessary qualification.

Save capture date, build, guidance links and export revision together. Revisit them after an interface change. After publication, inspect the real listing or page: a successful local export only proves that a file exists.

title: Screen Recording Privacy Checklist for Software Demos
description: Audit accounts, tabs, notifications, exports and sample data with a practical exposure and retake decision table.
lede: Audit accounts, tabs, notifications, exports and sample data with a practical exposure and retake decision table.
intent: Recording exposure review; not legal certification or the general capture tutorial.

sections.heading: Prepare a demonstration path
paragraphs: List every screen you will visit. Use an approved demonstration account with deliberately fictional data where possible. A clean opening dashboard does not guarantee that menus, suggestions or downloads are safe.

Use an invented workspace and a reserved example address such as alex@example.com for planning. Do not substitute real customer details in a public example. Confirm organizational rules with the responsible owner.

sections.heading: Inspect surrounding surfaces
paragraphs: Review browser profiles, tabs, bookmarks, desktop, file pickers and recent items. Check notification settings. Record a short rehearsal and inspect the complete interval before a full take.

Exposure can happen during a transition. Do not assume an editor’s final crop covers every frame. Check the moments before and after the central task, including windows opened temporarily to locate a file.

sections.heading: Decide whether to replace, redact or retake
paragraphs: Replacing data before capture is easier to review than chasing it through moving footage. If exposure is found, stop distribution of that revision and identify the affected intervals.

Retake when sensitive content moves, appears in several places or cannot be reliably removed. If redaction is used, inspect the actual export around every affected frame. One still with an aligned blur is not proof of continuous coverage.

sections.heading: Audit the handoff and response path
paragraphs: Review audio, captions, thumbnails, filenames and attached originals as well as the video. An internal-review folder and a public download can have different requirements. Attach approval to the exact shared revision.

Know who can remove or replace hosted copies. Follow the owner’s incident procedure if an exposure is discovered later; replacing a source does not remove every distributed copy. This checklist supports editorial review, not a legal determination that disclosure is permitted.

title: Make a Silent App Demo Understandable Without Sound
description: Plan a sound-off demonstration with visible actions, result states, a comprehension check and an accessibility review worksheet.
lede: Plan a sound-off demonstration with visible actions, result states, a comprehension check and an accessibility review worksheet.
intent: Visual task comprehension; text styling belongs to the readable-text guide.

sections.heading: Choose a task with a visible ending
paragraphs: “Save an article to Weekend reads” has an observable ending. “Organize your life” does not. Choose an action the interface can prove without narration.

This fictional reading-app sequence contains an article, a collection chooser and a saved confirmation. It is a planning model, not an existing product recording or a promise that UGC Pilot performs these app actions.

sections.heading: Separate instruction from result
paragraphs: “Choose a collection” tells viewers what to watch; it does not prove a save occurred. Hold on the actual saved state and keep the collection name consistent.

Do not substitute an animated check mark for product confirmation. If the interface lacks a clear confirmation, show the item in its actual destination or choose another task. Added graphics must not manufacture evidence.

sections.heading: Reduce simultaneous reading demands
paragraphs: Avoid dense overlays while viewers search a menu. Put the instruction before the action or hold the state long enough for both to be understood. Keep the cursor away from critical words.

A silent edit is not simply a narrated edit with its volume removed. Replace essential spoken context with visible context, then remove redundant labels. Review placement and contrast in the separate readable-text guide.

sections.heading: Test understanding and accessible alternatives
paragraphs: Play the export without sound for someone who has not read the script. Ask what was saved, where it went and how they know. Record their actual answers before explaining the intended story. Wrong answers reveal missing orientation or result evidence.

Sound-off clarity does not satisfy every accessibility need. Consider captions for meaningful audio in narrated versions and an accessible text explanation of important visuals. Use W3C guidance for the context; do not claim that a silent export alone makes the complete experience accessible.

title: SaaS Video CTA Examples: Choose the Next Step by Viewer Intent
description: Choose a demo-video next step using original CTA examples, destination checks and a viewer-stage decision matrix.
lede: Choose a demo-video next step using original CTA examples, destination checks and a viewer-stage decision matrix.
intent: Stage-matched destination selection; not the script template or generic persuasion.

sections.heading: Choose the destination before the words
paragraphs: A call to action should identify a useful next step that the viewer can actually complete. Decide the destination first: a worked example, a relevant feature page, a trial setup flow or an existing-user control. Then write the invitation.

The examples below are original illustrative copy, not tested winners. Use a row only when its destination and product conditions are true. “Try the sample project” is misleading if the product has no sample project.

sections.heading: Match the request to what the viewer knows
paragraphs: An unfamiliar viewer may need to understand one task before signing up. Someone comparing options may want the full workflow or relevant plan details. An existing user watching a feature update may only need to find the new control.

Do not make every clip end with the same signup demand. Conversely, do not send a ready user through several unrelated articles. Choose one primary action and make the destination continue the exact task the video introduced.

sections.heading: Make the promise concrete and qualified
paragraphs: “Open the setup checklist” explains the destination better than “Unlock your potential.” If a trial requires payment details, a feature needs a particular plan or a workflow needs an existing account, review the wording accordingly.

Avoid invented urgency and unsupported free, instant or unlimited claims. A clear invitation can be compelling without promising a result the app cannot guarantee. Keep the final frame, spoken ending, caption and clickable link consistent.

sections.heading: Verify the route as a visitor
paragraphs: Open the destination signed out, on a phone and, when relevant, in an eligible existing account. Check redirects, login requirements and whether the referenced item is present. Record what happens for someone who cannot access the feature.

Measure the action only if reliable tracking exists. A click is not proof that setup finished, and a signup is not proof that the viewer achieved the demonstrated result. Keep those stages separate when judging whether the ending helped.

title: Product Demo vs Explainer Video: Choose by the Viewer’s Question
description: Use a decision tree and paired fictional briefs to choose between a product demo, explainer, tutorial and feature announcement.
lede: Use a decision tree and paired fictional briefs to choose between a product demo, explainer, tutorial and feature announcement.
intent: Choose the appropriate communication format; not compare video software vendors.

sections.heading: Start with the unresolved question
paragraphs: If viewers ask what a problem is and why a product category matters, an explainer may help. If they ask whether your product can perform a task, a demo needs visible product evidence. If they ask how to complete that task themselves, a tutorial should preserve the necessary steps.
These are useful editorial distinctions, not rigid industry definitions. Real assets can combine formats. Choose a primary job so the opening and ending do not compete.

sections.heading: Compare two briefs for the same fictional product
paragraphs: Imagine a fictional booking app for independent tutors. An explainer brief asks: why do missed scheduling details cause confusion? Its outline introduces the problem, describes a shared booking process and gives a qualified next step. It must not invent customer losses to make the problem dramatic.

A demo brief asks: can a tutor change a sample appointment and see the updated booking? Its outline shows the current slot, the real rescheduling control and the confirmed new time. That visible change is evidence an abstract explainer cannot supply.

sections.heading: Choose the evidence before the production style
paragraphs: The same camera style, animation or presenter could appear in either format. An AI presenter does not turn a generic explanation into a product demonstration. Likewise, a screen recording without a clear task may fail to demonstrate anything useful.

Write the claim and the evidence needed to support it. For a tutorial, add prerequisites and recovery steps. For an announcement, add release eligibility. If the necessary evidence does not exist, narrow the brief rather than decorating an unsupported claim.

sections.heading: Avoid building two pages or videos that answer the same thing
paragraphs: If an existing demo already explains the booking task, do not make a second asset with a different label but identical substance. Add the missing prerequisite or context to the existing asset unless the audience’s question truly differs.

Ask a reviewer which question the proposed video answers and what they can do next. If the answer shifts between category education, feature proof and setup instructions, choose one primary purpose and link to the appropriate follow-up.

sections.heading: Collect questions with permission and context
paragraphs: Use approved support notes, interviews or your own review of the product. Keep the question’s task and user state while removing identifying details. Do not publish private tickets or imply that a fictional example came from a real customer.
Every row below is invented to demonstrate triage. It is not a claim about question frequency. Add actual counts only when a reliable, permissioned record supports them.

sections.heading: Decide whether video is the right answer
paragraphs: Video is useful when a visible sequence, state change or hard-to-find control answers the question. A billing date, access rule or changing policy is often better handled by maintained text and a direct help link.

A recurring question can also reveal a product or documentation defect. Sending more people to a clip is not always the best fix. Record whether the underlying label, empty state or help page needs an owner before selecting a content task.

sections.heading: Merge questions by their underlying task
paragraphs: “Where are my call notes?” and “How do I open Monday’s note?” may belong to one find-a-note demonstration. “Can I export my notes?” needs different evidence. Merge based on the action and result, not shared keywords.
Keep the original questions in a private, appropriately sanitized planning log and give the public asset a clear task title. Avoid creating separate near-identical pages for every wording variant.

sections.heading: Write a brief and close the loop
paragraphs: For the selected task, specify starting state, necessary steps, visible result and a relevant help destination. Have a reviewer who resembles the intended user attempt the task from the video. Record where they still need clarification.

When the answer changes, update the source help page and video together. A dated demo of an old interface can create new support work. Track an owner and review trigger, such as a navigation change, instead of assuming publication completes the job.

sections.heading: Choose one task with a stable result
paragraphs: A useful tutorial carousel lets someone repeat a real workflow. Use one task and a consistent sample object. This fictional notes-app example teaches how to locate a call note and identify its next step; it is not an actual product screenshot or customer result.

Keep the prerequisite close to the beginning: the viewer needs a workspace containing the sample note. If your app has another starting state, rewrite the sequence instead of assuming the same navigation.

sections.heading: Pair each slide with one visible instruction
paragraphs: The seven-slide table provides original copy and evidence directions. Capture the real interface for your product. Highlight one relevant control without covering its label, and retain enough context to orient the viewer.

Do not use a generated dashboard as proof that a feature works. If a screenshot needs annotations, distinguish the annotation from actual UI. A drawn arrow should help locate the control; it should not impersonate a product confirmation.

sections.heading: Review the sequence as instructions
paragraphs: Check the slide order against the live workflow. A missing prerequisite can make a beautiful carousel unusable. Include a truthful recovery instruction for a missing note or unavailable control rather than promising identical results for every account.

Use consistent labels and make the resulting next step readable at normal phone size. Avoid adding a second teaching task merely to fill a slide count. Seven is the length of this example, not a required format.

sections.heading: Provide context outside the image
paragraphs: Write accompanying text that explains the task and links to maintained instructions. Add meaningful text alternatives where the publishing surface supports them. Do not rely only on arrows, color or screenshots to communicate the action.

Before sharing, ask a fresh reviewer to follow the carousel in an eligible account. Record the point where they hesitate. Revise that instruction or image, then check the actual export and destination rather than only the design canvas.

title: Mobile App Onboarding Video: Teach the First Meaningful Action
description: Plan a post-signup tutorial with prerequisites, permission alternatives, empty states, recovery paths and a visible completion check.
lede: Plan a post-signup tutorial with prerequisites, permission alternatives, empty states, recovery paths and a visible completion check.
intent: Post-signup first-use assistance, not acquisition or a store preview.

sections.heading: Define completion from the user’s perspective
paragraphs: Pick a first action that makes the app useful: save a first reading item, create a first project or complete a sample session. Opening the home screen is not necessarily meaningful completion. Choose one action and confirm how the app visibly records it.
This example uses a fictional reading app. The user creates a collection and saves a first article. It does not describe a UGC Pilot feature or evidence of improved activation.

sections.heading: Show the real starting state
paragraphs: State whether the viewer must already have an account, a verified email or a workspace invitation. Capture the actual first-use screen rather than an established account full of content. A populated account can conceal the decisions that make onboarding difficult.
If the app offers a sample item, identify it as sample content. Do not imply that every new account already contains imported personal data. Use a setup path that the intended role can access.

sections.heading: Handle permissions, waiting and recovery
paragraphs: A permission request needs an honest explanation and, where the product supports one, a useful alternative. Do not imply a person must grant an optional permission to continue. For this fictional reading task, pasting an article link might be a supported alternative to browser integration. Verify that alternative in your actual app.

Show loading as loading and failure as failure. A cut that removes every wait can imply a speed guarantee. When a request fails, link to the real retry or help path rather than creating an invented success screen.

sections.heading: Confirm success and keep the tutorial current
paragraphs: End on the saved article inside the chosen collection, not on a decorative celebration. Ask a new reviewer to repeat the task and explain how they know it completed. Check the path for both empty and already-populated accounts if both are relevant.

Keep the tutorial version tied to the app build and starting state. Update it when labels, permissions or prerequisites change. Track completion separately from video views when reliable measurement exists; watching does not prove the user finished setup.

title: Product Demo Hook Testing: Compare Openings Without Changing Everything
description: Use a controlled creative brief, observation log and interpretation checklist to compare demo openings without inventing winners.
lede: Use a controlled creative brief, observation log and interpretation checklist to compare demo openings without inventing winners.
intent: A measurement protocol for openings, not a list of hooks or guaranteed viral advice.

sections.heading: Write a narrow question before making variants
paragraphs: Ask whether a task-specific opening helps your intended viewers recognize the demo. For a fictional notes app, compare A: “Where did Monday’s next step go?” with B: “Find your next step before the follow-up.” Both must lead to the same real find-a-note demonstration.

These are original creative candidates, not proven hooks. Do not label either a winner before collecting observations. If you want to test a facial reaction, keep the words fixed in that separate comparison.

sections.heading: Hold the rest of the creative stable
paragraphs: Use the same demo, result, ending, captions, aspect ratio and destination. Record which opening words, image or timing changed. Changing several elements makes it difficult to identify a useful next revision.
Keep a copy of each actual export. Similar filenames are not proof that the body stayed unchanged. Review both side by side before release and write down any unavoidable difference.

sections.heading: Choose available metrics and a review window
paragraphs: Use the reporting actually available for the destination. YouTube provides audience-retention reporting, but availability and processing can affect what you see. Consult the official report guidance and note which fields are present.

Record the exact metric definition. YouTube Shorts distinguishes views and engaged views; counts using different definitions should not be treated as the same measurement. Do not combine platform metrics into a single invented retention score. Choose a review window in advance and allow reporting to settle.

sections.heading: Interpret observations with their limits
paragraphs: Organic posts are rarely randomized. Different viewers, timing, distribution and sample sizes can explain differences. Record reach and audience context beside retention observations. A larger view count alone does not demonstrate that the opening caused improvement.

Use the log to choose another careful test, not to claim universal superiority. If information is sparse or definitions differ, mark the result inconclusive. Keep a truthful description such as “variant B had a different observed pattern in this window” and avoid causal claims the setup cannot support.

title: Review AI UGC Footage Before Adding a Software Demo
description: Apply an acceptance and rejection rubric for presenter footage, software evidence, exact text, continuity and export review.
lede: Apply an acceptance and rejection rubric for presenter footage, software evidence, exact text, continuity and export review.
intent: Detailed output inspection and rejection actions; not the broad AI generator explanation.

sections.heading: Separate presenter footage from software proof
paragraphs: An AI presenter or reaction can introduce a task. It cannot establish that a software feature exists. Use genuine approved app recordings for product evidence and keep generated interface pixels out of the proof sequence.

The failure cases below are original illustrative review scenarios. They are not results from generated clips, provider evaluations or proof that a particular model passes or fails. Actual footage still needs a real review.

sections.heading: Inspect identity, motion and contact points
paragraphs: Watch at normal speed, then inspect suspicious intervals frame by frame. Compare the presenter against the approved identity reference where one is used. Look for changes in facial structure, clothing, hands, object contact, background geometry and motion continuity.

Pause at the beginning, end and transitions. A convincing still does not establish that the complete clip is usable. Record timestamps and the specific observed problem rather than writing “looks off.” Keep source scene instructions and identity references distinct in the review record.

sections.heading: Treat text and claims as separate gates
paragraphs: Check every visible and spoken claim against the real product and eligibility. Exact captions should be reviewed as editable text and again in the export; do not assume generated lettering is accurate. Avoid simulated testimonials, invented customers and unsupported outcome claims.

When a face or gesture is acceptable but a claim is wrong, changing the music does not fix it. Correct the script or edit the problematic interval. When the footage itself fails, reject that segment rather than hiding a defect behind fast cuts.

sections.heading: Record the decision on the actual revision
paragraphs: Use accept, revise or reject with a reason and timestamp. Accept only the use case actually reviewed: an approved reaction shot does not approve a longer narration or a new product claim. Keep source, edit and export revisions linked.

Finally watch the joined presenter-and-demo export on desktop and phone, with and without sound. Check the transition into genuine software footage and the next-step destination. title: How to Combine an AI Reaction Hook with a Real SaaS Demo
description: Plan a reaction hook and real app demo as one social video, with a worked SaaS example, timed edit plan and UGC Pilot workflow checklist.
lede: Use the opening to make a founder’s problem recognizable, then let a real recording of your app answer it. The reaction and the demonstration should tell the same story.
intent: A complete social reaction-to-product-proof format; existing editing guide owns general demo shortening.

sections.heading: What the hook-plus-demo format actually does
paragraphs: A hook-plus-demo video has two connected parts: a short reaction that introduces a problem or discovery, followed by real software footage showing the useful action. The first part gives someone a reason to watch. The second supplies the evidence. An expressive face cannot prove that an app works.

For a SaaS founder, the starting question is not which reaction looks most dramatic. It is which specific product action deserves attention. Choose that action first, then write an opening that the demonstration can honestly answer. This is a creative format to test, not a promise of viral reach.

sections.heading: Build the message from a business fact
paragraphs: Consider NorthStar Notes, a fictional notes app used only for this worked example. Its intended audience is small teams following up on client calls. The example assumes that a project contains call notes and each note includes a next-step section. It does not assume automatic follow-up messages, saved hours or improved sales.

The opening candidate is: “why am i still digging through every call note?” The demo then opens a sample project, selects Monday’s call and shows its next step. Replace that line and sequence with your own verified product behavior. If your app cannot show the answer, change the hook rather than invent a screen.

The diagram and timed plan below are original illustrative planning aids. They are not generated footage, customer testimony or a recording of a tested NorthStar product. The sample timings describe an editorial cut; they are not model-duration limits or a recommended length for every video.

sections.heading: Choose an opening that leaves room for the product
paragraphs: Use an owned reaction clip or an AI-generated opening that fits the message. A puzzled look can introduce searching for information; a small realization can introduce a useful discovery. An unrelated shocked performance makes a larger promise than a modest software action can repay.

In UGC Pilot, the Hook video workflow has a Create area for footage and a Demo step for the product recording. If requesting new AI footage, review the available model, supported references and displayed credit estimate before submitting. An existing owned opening can avoid an unnecessary new generation. Do not treat a reference clip as permission to republish its creator or claims.

Keep exact hook wording in an editable text layer. Generated lettering is not a reliable substitute for approved copy. If an identity reference is used, review the person’s appearance separately from whether the scene and performance support your message. A generated reaction should not be presented as a genuine customer endorsement.

sections.heading: Attach the real app recording in Demo
paragraphs: Record only the steps needed to answer the hook, using safe sample data. Keep the selected project, call and result recognizable. Do not replace genuine product footage with an invented interface or hide an important prerequisite behind a fast cut.

After choosing the opening, move to Demo and use Upload demo or the available saved-demo selection. Review the selected file before trimming it. The relevant selection is your actual app recording, not another reaction clip. If it is a desktop capture, frame the important control and result so they remain readable on a phone.

Review opening and demo as one sequence. A preview of an individual clip is not evidence that the final joined video is correct. If finishing options are unavailable in your account, keep the source assets and use an editor that can complete the sequence; do not assume that a successful generation has also rendered your product demo.

sections.heading: Make the reveal answer the opening
paragraphs: At the cut into the app, retain a clear visual bridge: the same task name, a brief instruction or the selected object. In the fictional example, a label such as “open Monday’s call” is more useful than another vague reaction. Hold on the actual next step long enough for someone to read it.

Keep the ending proportional to what was shown. “See how call notes are organized” is a better invitation for this example than an unsupported promise to automate a whole team’s follow-up. Check that the destination continues the same task. A trial invitation is appropriate only when that trial is actually available.

sections.heading: Review the exported social video
paragraphs: Watch the actual export at normal phone size, once with sound and once without. Check the hook words, source selection, cut point, readable controls, final result and next step. If captions or other audio are included, review them independently; do not infer spoken content from silent footage.

Ask a fresh reviewer what problem the opening raised and what the app did to answer it. If those answers differ, revise the message or sequence before sharing. Their feedback is a useful comprehension check, not a measured claim about retention, signups or future performance.

To compare another opening later, keep the product recording and ending unchanged. Record what changed and use the reporting actually available to you. Different organic audiences and posting times can affect observations, so a higher view count alone does not establish a better hook.

title: How to Make a Wall-of-Text Video for Your SaaS
description: Turn verified SaaS business context into a natural wall-of-text social video, with original overlay copy, a footage plan and a UGC Pilot checklist.
lede: Let one relatable situation carry the message. Write the words from real business context, choose footage that leaves them readable, and review the text as part of the final video.
intent: Business-context-to-written-social-story workflow; existing readable-text guide owns typography and existing hook library owns short openings.

sections.heading: Choose this format when the written message carries the story
paragraphs: A wall-of-text video puts a compact written story, observation or list over moving footage. The words do most of the explaining. The background creates a fitting mood and gives the frame some life. It is different from a short hook followed by a product recording, and different from subtitles transcribing speech.

For a SaaS or app business, the useful story is a situation the intended viewer recognizes. Start with a task, frustration or discovery connected to a real feature. “Our platform is revolutionary” gives people little to picture. A specific follow-up task gives the text a scene and a reason for the product to appear.

sections.heading: Separate business facts from the creative angle
paragraphs: Use the same fictional NorthStar Notes example as the hook-plus-demo guide: small teams keep call notes inside projects and can read a next-step section in a chosen note. These are assumed facts for the exercise, not an existing customer case study. Do not add automatic reminders, integrations or time savings to make the story sound stronger.

The creative angle is the moment between finishing a call and preparing the follow-up. That is a writing choice. It is not evidence that a real person used the app or achieved a result. If your business context comes from a profile or an AI text suggestion, check each product statement against the actual app before using it.

The table below shows how the brief becomes complete overlay copy. The writing is an original illustrative candidate, not a transcribed creator post or a tested high-performing video. No generation or campaign result is implied.

sections.heading: Use one complete overlay instead of a pile of slogans
paragraphs:
Here is the example overlay, with intentional paragraph breaks: “the call is over.
the follow-up is tomorrow.
and the next step is somewhere in your notes.

NorthStar Notes keeps the call note and its next steps together.
open the project, choose the call, check what comes next.”

The first lines establish a situation. The product mention explains the relevant behavior. The ending names the action without claiming an outcome the app cannot prove. Replace the brand, situation and action together when adapting it; changing only a product name leaves generic copy.

First-person copy needs extra care. If you write “I tried this” or “this saved me hours,” those words imply an experience. Use them only when they truthfully represent the speaker and have support. A natural style does not require a fabricated testimonial.

sections.heading: Choose a background that supports reading
paragraphs: Pick owned or appropriately permissioned footage with a calm enough region for the overlay. A reaction, an everyday work moment or another relevant background can work if it does not demand attention away from the words. Busy gestures, abrupt cuts and competing signs can make the paragraph difficult to follow.

A generated background is illustrative footage, not evidence that someone uses your SaaS. Keep the exact overlay out of the generated pixels and add it as editable text. Choose the available duration based on a real reading rehearsal rather than squeezing the paragraph into the shortest output.

If the message genuinely needs several screens of product proof, consider hook-plus-demo or a slideshow instead. A dense overlay does not have to carry an entire product tour. Shorten the editorial scope or change format rather than making the text too small.

sections.heading: Build and review it in UGC Pilot
paragraphs: Open Wall of text in Explore. Choose an owned background or create footage with the available controls. Review any displayed credit estimate before a new generation. A source reference helps you plan a creative structure; it does not establish permission to reuse another creator’s footage, wording or claims.

For the chosen video, use the text-editing area to add or review your overlay. Keep the selected words and paragraph breaks deliberate. If using a text remix, confirm that it refers to your business and preserves only supported product facts. A useful draft is still a draft.

Review the preview, then inspect the final output. Check placement, reading time and contrast over the whole moving scene. The simple text editor and any advanced editing controls serve different jobs; use the controls available in your account instead of assuming every generation is already a finished, shareable asset.

sections.heading: Give the viewer a truthful next step
paragraphs: A text-led story can mention the product naturally without forcing a separate sales line into every paragraph. If you add a destination in the accompanying post or on the page, make it relevant to the feature the words describe. Do not invent a free offer or a download deadline for urgency.

Before sharing, ask someone to read the exported video once at normal phone size and summarize it. They should be able to name the situation and the actual product behavior. If they remember only the frustration, clarify the connection; if they cannot finish reading, revise the copy or available reading time.

Keep the approved words and final revision so the next variation changes a deliberate element: situation, tone, background or product angle. Treat watch and response data as observations with platform-specific definitions. These examples offer creative starting points, not a guarantee of viral distribution.

title: Match a reaction hook to the feature your SaaS demo proves
description: Choose a reaction hook that sets up the exact feature a SaaS demo can show, using a simple message-match check and fictional examples.
lede: Choose a reaction hook that sets up the exact feature a SaaS demo can show, using a simple message-match check and fictional examples.

sections.heading: Start with the proof, then write the hook
paragraphs: A reaction can earn attention, but the next shot needs to answer the question it raises. Before writing an opening, name the screen, action and visible result your recording actually shows. Then write the hook around that same result. A general reaction such as “wait, look at this” needs a precise caption or an immediate visual reveal to make its promise clear.

Use this fictional planning example: NorthStar Notes lets a team open a project call note and read its next-step section. That is an assumed feature for this exercise, not evidence about a customer or a product result.

sections.heading: Check the promise against the screen
paragraphs: Suppose the opening says “my follow-ups write themselves,” but the demo only opens a note containing next steps. That promises automatic writing the recording does not prove. Replace it with “wait, the next steps are right here,” then show the note and highlight its next-step section. The second line is less sweeping and matches the visible action.

Check a second mismatch: “all my meetings in one place” leads into a clip showing one note. Either show the actual meeting list if the app has it, or narrow the hook to “the next step from this call.” Do not infer an integration or automatic behavior from an attractive screen.

sections.heading: Make the match easy to see
paragraphs: List the main noun and verb in your hook: for example, “next steps” and “find.” Find the same noun on screen and the action that makes it visible. If the match takes explanation, add a short bridge label such as “open the call note” or change the shot order. Keep the actual recording readable and use only a test account or content you can share.

After drafting, show someone the first two shots without explaining them. Ask what they expected and what the clip showed. If those answers differ, revise the opening or record more proof. This is a practical review exercise, not a claim that any hook will go viral.

sections.heading: Choose one recognizable moment
paragraphs: Start with a specific situation the intended viewer may recognize, not a broad claim that everyone has the same problem. The strongest material is a task, a moment of uncertainty and a practical next step. Ask what people actually do before they reach for your feature; if you do not know, use a neutral hypothetical rather than pretending to quote a customer.

The fictional example here is a team preparing to follow up after a call. The example app, NorthStar Notes, has a project call note with a next-step section. These assumed facts illustrate a writing method and are not a customer testimonial.

sections.heading: Write the situation before the product
paragraphs:
A possible overlay is: “the call ended.
the follow-up is tomorrow.
and the next step is somewhere in the notes.

open the project note.
check the next-step section.
start from there.” This uses short, ordinary sentences and gives the viewer an action. It does not say a real person experienced the problem or achieved a measurable result.

To include the product, add “NorthStar Notes keeps the call note and next steps together” only if your own app can actually do the equivalent. Replace the task and product fact as a pair, so the copy reflects your business rather than simply swapping a brand name.

sections.heading: Avoid invented first-person proof
paragraphs: “I lost three hours looking for this” sounds like a personal account. Use it only if the speaker really had that experience and is comfortable making the statement. “Ever finish a call and wonder what comes next?” is a question rather than a fabricated event, though it still needs to be relevant to the audience. Avoid unsupported time savings, guarantees and fake review language.

If a claim needs verification, write the fact you need in a separate note and check it in the product or with the person involved. Remove the claim if you cannot support it. You can create curiosity without making a promise about the outcome.

sections.heading: Edit for a moving background
paragraphs: Read the full overlay once at normal phone size over the intended clip. Break lines at natural phrases, keep the contrast strong and use a calm region of the frame. If the message cannot be read comfortably, shorten it or allow more time. Add the exact copy in an editor rather than relying on a video generator to spell it correctly.

Compare the final export with the approved words and check that the moving footage does not cover or compete with the text. A generated reaction or workspace scene illustrates the situation; it is not evidence that a real user had this experience.

sections.heading: Start with the same facts
paragraphs: A wall-of-text format can be a compact paragraph, a stacked list or a point-of-view scene. Choose the form based on the job the words need to do, not merely the amount of text. The fictional brief below assumes an app keeps a call note and its next steps together. These are example facts, not claims about a real customer or performance.
The viewer is a team member preparing a follow-up. The useful action is opening the note and checking the next-step section. Keep those same facts when comparing the three versions.

sections.heading: Write three forms from one brief
paragraphs: Paragraph: “the call is over and the follow-up is tomorrow. open the project note and check the next-step section before you start.” This reads like a short thought and connects the situation to one action.

Stacked list: “after the call:
open the project
find the call note
check the next steps.” The list is useful when the order of actions is the message. Check that every action is supported by the actual product.

POV: “pov: you finish the call, open the project note, and the next steps are right where you left them.” This creates a scene. It should not imply a real testimonial or claim that the product created those steps automatically.

sections.heading: Select by what the viewer must retain
paragraphs: Choose the paragraph when the relationship between a situation and an action needs a complete sentence. Choose the list for a genuinely ordered set of steps. Choose POV for a single scene that needs a recognizable setup. If the viewer must understand a complex interaction, a short demo or multi-slide tutorial may be clearer than any dense overlay.

Read each option aloud and remove duplicate phrases. Check whether the first line makes the topic clear without hiding the useful action until the very end. Do not expand a list with extra steps simply to fill the screen.

sections.heading: Fit the copy to real footage
paragraphs: Keep the chosen words in a separate editable text layer. Preview them over the entire clip: a quiet background at the beginning may become busy later. Adjust line breaks and timing so the words stay legible, and verify the final export against the approved version.

Test comprehension with someone who has not seen the draft: ask what task the text describes and what action comes next. This review can uncover ambiguity; it does not establish that one format will outperform the others.

sections.heading: Choose one point of view
paragraphs: A POV overlay places the viewer inside a recognizable situation. Select one person, one moment and one task before writing. It is a creative setup, not proof that a customer had the experience. If the message requires a real testimonial, use only an actual account with permission.

For this fictional planning exercise, NorthStar Notes organizes a project call note with a next-step section. Imagine a teammate preparing a follow-up after a call. No customer, performance result or product usage is claimed.

paragraphs: Try this overlay: “pov: the call is done, the follow-up is tomorrow, and you cannot remember which note had the next step.
you open the project note and find the next-step section.
okay, now you know where to start.” The first line establishes the scene; the middle gives a specific action; the last closes the moment without promising an outcome.
For a task-management app, use a different situation: “pov: monday starts and you are looking for the task your team agreed to finish.

paragraphs: A hypothetical “pov: you…” can describe an imagined scenario. “I used this and saved hours” is a personal and measurable assertion. If the next-step section must be manually written, the copy must not suggest the app creates it automatically.

If a reference inspired the structure, write your own wording and keep a record of the reference and its permissions. A familiar creative structure does not give you the right to reuse a creator’s video or exact text.

sections.heading: Give the product a reason to appear
paragraphs: A product mention feels connected when it helps the viewer understand a specific task in the story. Start with the viewer’s situation, then name a single behavior the app actually supports. You do not need to insert the brand into every line, and a product name is not a substitute for an explanation.
The fictional example uses NorthStar Notes: a call note contains a next-step section. This is an invented planning brief, not a real customer example.

sections.heading: Compare a broad claim with a useful rewrite
paragraphs: Heavy-handed draft: “Stop wasting time. NorthStar Notes is the ultimate all-in-one productivity app that fixes your meetings.” It is unclear what the app does, and “fixes your meetings” is an unsupported outcome.
Rewritten overlay: “the call ends. the follow-up is tomorrow.
open the project note in NorthStar Notes. the next-step section is in the same note.
start with the next action.” This names the relevant screen and fact. It does not assert that the app generates the next steps or that a user saved time.

sections.heading: Decide whether the name belongs in the overlay
paragraphs: Include the name when it helps explain the action or distinguish the product being shown. Leave it out when the visual already identifies the app and the story reads better without repetition. If the viewer needs a next step, use an accurate destination in the accompanying post or link; do not promise a free feature, automatic workflow or outcome unless it is true.

When adapting the example, replace the task and feature together. For a scheduling app, “choose a date and review the available time” is only accurate if those controls exist in your product. Check claims and availability before the copy goes live.

sections.heading: Review the complete edit
paragraphs: Keep the approved text in an editable layer, and pair it with owned or permissioned footage. A generated background may illustrate a situation but does not prove that a person used your product. If using a product recording, remove private information and show the relevant screen long enough to understand it.

On a phone, read the overlay once while the footage plays. Check spelling, line breaks, contrast and the final export. If the brand mention interrupts the story, remove or reposition it and ask whether the viewer can still identify the next action.

sections.heading: Start with a question you can answer
paragraphs: Choose an objection or uncertainty that a potential user may have, then identify what your product can actually show in response. Prefer a question you have heard with permission to use it. Otherwise label it as a hypothetical planning example; do not present it as a customer quote. Avoid answering a broad concern with a feature that does not resolve it.

This fictional example assumes NorthStar Notes keeps a call note and a next-step section together. The hypothetical question is: “Where do I find the next steps after a call?” The example is not a customer interview.

sections.heading: Write an explanation and a screen action
paragraphs: A short script could be: “If you need the next steps from a call, open the project and choose the call note. The next-step section is in that note.” Show the project view, opening the note and the relevant section as the words describe them. If the actual app requires more steps, show or explain those steps rather than hiding them.

A weak answer would be “our AI automatically handles all your follow-ups” over the same recording. The visible note does not establish automatic writing, delivery or completion. Remove those claims unless your product actually supports them and the proof is shown.

sections.heading: Make speech and evidence agree
paragraphs: Create a two-column review before filming: each spoken sentence on one side and the corresponding screen or source on the other. Delete or qualify a sentence that has no supporting evidence. Use a sample account or obtain permission for any real information shown. If the question involves price, privacy or a feature limit, check current product documentation rather than guessing.
A generated presenter can deliver an illustrative script, but it is not a real customer endorsing the product. Make the speaker’s role clear and do not invent a personal experience or outcome.

sections.heading: Review the handoff and finish
paragraphs: When the speaker says “choose the call note,” the recording should show the relevant click or a clear resulting screen. Avoid covering the control with subtitles, and give viewers enough time to read the result. If the action is difficult to see, crop or rerecord the screen while retaining context.

Check the final export on a phone and compare the spoken script, captions and screen. Ask someone unfamiliar with the product whether the original question was answered. A successful review shows clarity, not evidence of conversions or guaranteed performance.

sections.heading: Pick one problem and one supported response
paragraphs: A problem-solution slideshow works when each slide advances a single idea. Define the intended reader, a task they recognize and a product action that responds to it. Check the real feature before writing; a carousel should not promise an outcome the product cannot demonstrate.
This fictional example uses NorthStar Notes, which has a project call note with a next-step section. It is an illustrative creative brief, not an actual customer case or tested campaign.

sections.heading: Plan a complete five-slide sequence
paragraphs: Slide 1 — “The call is over. Where did the next step go?” This establishes a specific moment rather than a generic productivity promise.

Slide 2 — “You have the notes. Now you need the action you agreed on.” This clarifies the reader’s task. Slide 3 — “Open the project and choose the call note.” This introduces the first actual action.

Slide 4 — “Check the next-step section in the same note.” Pair it with a readable, sanitized view of that section if your real app supports it. Slide 5 — “Start with the next step.” Give the reader a relevant route to learn more if one exists. These are planning words, not evidence that a user achieved a result.

sections.heading: Give each slide a visual job
paragraphs: The opening can use a simple situation-focused visual. Use a project view for the action and a note view for the feature; do not use a generated interface as proof of what the application does. A real screenshot must come from an account and data you are allowed to share. Mark up only the relevant control and keep surrounding context readable.

If the product cannot show a project note or next-step section, rewrite the sequence around a feature it can actually demonstrate. Avoid invented automation, quantified savings, customer quotations and universal results.

sections.heading: Review the sequence as one story
paragraphs: Read the slides in order without an explanation. Can a reader describe the problem, the relevant action and what to do next? Remove a slide if it only repeats another. If the sequence instead teaches multiple detailed steps, a tutorial may be the more useful structure.

Preview at phone size, check contrast and text placement, then inspect the actual export. Test links and any destination separately before sharing. A clear sequence is an editorial starting point, not a promise of reach or conversion.

sections.heading: Record the structure without importing its claims
paragraphs: A reference can suggest a sequence: a reaction, a problem, a screen action and a closing line. That structure is different from the original creator’s exact words, footage, identity, product facts and performance claims. Describe what each part does in neutral terms before drafting your own concept.

This is an invented planning example, not an analysis of an actual creator video: a reference outline might begin with surprise, then show a software action. The outline tells you nothing about whether the same action or result exists in your product.

sections.heading: Rewrite from your own product facts
paragraphs: Assume the fictional reference claims “the app automatically sends my follow-ups.” Your product might only display a next-step section in a saved note. Do not reuse that claim or imply automatic sending. A suitable original direction could be: “wait, the next steps are in the note,” followed by a real recording that opens that section.

Write three columns: the role of the reference segment, the fact or claim it makes, and the verified fact available for your own product. If there is no matching fact, change the message or reject the concept. Changing a brand name does not turn an unsupported claim into a supported one.

sections.heading: Respect the reference and the speaker
paragraphs: Keep a record of the source and whether you have permission for any asset you intend to reuse. A link or screenshot alone does not establish rights; seek permission or use your own licensed materials. Create original wording and footage instead of assuming another creator’s transcript or likeness is available to copy.

Do not present an invented AI speaker as a real user or claim personal experience they did not have. If you use a real testimonial or customer story, verify the exact quote and obtain appropriate consent.

sections.heading: Check the finished concept against evidence
paragraphs: Review each sentence alongside the real product view that supports it. If a feature is not visible, show it clearly or remove the assertion. If the product needs conditions or setup, include those conditions where they matter. Use sanitized, permissioned screen footage and review captions for accuracy.
Record the creative decision separately from any performance observation. A structure can be a useful experiment without demonstrating that your version will earn similar views, retention or sales.

sections.heading: Choose the reader’s job first
paragraphs: A story-led slideshow helps a viewer recognize a situation and understand why an action matters. A tutorial helps someone carry out a task in order. Both can use the same feature, but their slides should answer different questions. Start by deciding whether your reader needs context or instructions, then choose the sequence accordingly.
For this fictional exercise, NorthStar Notes has project call notes with a next-step section. The facts are assumptions for planning, not a description of a verified customer or an actual campaign.

sections.heading: Build the story version
paragraphs: Slide 1: “The call is over. The follow-up is tomorrow.” Slide 2: “The next action is somewhere in the notes.” Slide 3: “Open the project note and find the next-step section.” Slide 4: “Start from the action you agreed on.” The sequence moves from a moment to a response. It does not claim the app writes or sends the follow-up.

Use a visual that fits each moment, and show a real product screen only if you can record or capture one without private information. Generated background imagery can set a mood but does not prove how software works.

sections.heading: Build the tutorial version
paragraphs: Slide 1: “How to find the next steps from a call.” Slide 2: “Open the relevant project.” Slide 3: “Select the call note.” Slide 4: “Find its next-step section.” Slide 5: “Review the next action before following up.” Each slide has an ordered instruction rather than a narrative beat.

For your own product, verify every label and step using the current interface. If the steps are different, rewrite the tutorial. Add a screenshot only when it genuinely demonstrates the instruction, and avoid cropping out the context needed to understand the control.

sections.heading: Select and review
paragraphs: Choose the story when the main problem is unfamiliar or relatable context is essential. Choose the tutorial when the viewer already wants to complete the action. If the planned story merely restates every tutorial step, combine or revise rather than publishing two near-identical assets.

Read each version on a phone and ask an unfamiliar reader to explain what they learned. Check every claim, permission and destination before sharing. Neither structure guarantees better results; compare observations only after publishing, with the same measurement conditions where possible.

sections.heading: Start with one verified feature
paragraphs: A creative angle is the lens through which you explain the same product behavior. A matrix helps a founder compare situations and messages without inventing additional features. Write the audience, one supported feature and the evidence you can show first. Then explore a small number of angles rather than a large list of interchangeable hooks.
For this fictional exercise, NorthStar Notes lets a team open a project call note and read a next-step section. This assumption illustrates the method; it is not a customer result.

sections.heading: Draft three angles from the same facts
paragraphs: Frustration angle: “the call ended and the next step is somewhere in the notes.” Show the note and the relevant section. This addresses a task without claiming every viewer has the problem.
Discovery angle: “wait, the next-step section is in the same note.” Show the section as the line appears. This makes sense only if the real product actually places it there.

Use-case angle: “before the follow-up, open the project note and check the next step.” Show the action in sequence. It explains a practical use without implying that a follow-up is automatically generated or sent.

sections.heading: Pair each angle with an appropriate format
paragraphs: A reaction followed by real app footage can show the discovery. A wall-of-text overlay can describe the frustration, provided it is readable over the chosen footage. A slideshow can explain the use case one step at a time. These are planning options, not proof that any format performs better.

Write the actual opening, supporting proof and viewer action for each option. If two angles have the same opening and same proof, combine them; changing a few adjectives does not create a useful independent concept.

sections.heading: Choose one testable revision
paragraphs: Review all assertions against the product. Avoid fictional testimonials, automatic features not present in the app and unsupported savings. Make the first version using footage and content you have permission to use, then record the exact revision you want to compare next.

When examining results, note platform, audience, timing and available measures. Small or unequal samples and distribution differences make causal conclusions uncertain. The matrix records creative decisions; it does not predict reach.

sections.heading: Test the product fit before writing
paragraphs: A reference may look compelling while depending on a product behavior your app does not support. List its central promise, the action shown and the result implied. Then compare those items with your own verified feature and available proof. If the match is missing, change the concept or choose another reference; do not invent a capability to preserve the format.
The following is a fictional example for planning. It is not an analysis of a real creator or a claim about an existing business.

sections.heading: Reject the unsupported central claim
paragraphs: Imagine a reference that says “my follow-up sends itself” while showing an automatic send. Your fictional notes product can display next steps in a saved call note but cannot send a follow-up. A renamed copy of the reference would still mislead.

Keep only the general creative function if it fits: a brief reaction followed by a clear task. Replace the claim with “the next steps are in the note,” then show your own real note and section. If your application does not have that section either, choose another verified task.

sections.heading: Check whether the audience and format fit
paragraphs: A reference can also fail because it assumes a different viewer. A joke about a large sales team may not help a solo app founder understand your feature. Write the intended viewer and the task they need to complete. If the source’s setup requires knowledge your audience lacks, add context or choose another structure.

Consider whether the proof fits the format. A dense screen may need a slower tutorial or slideshow instead of a fast reaction cut. Do not crop away conditions or hide required setup just to imitate the pacing of a reference.

sections.heading: Keep a record of the decision
paragraphs: Record the reference link, the intended structural idea, unsupported claims you removed and your own supporting evidence. Obtain the necessary permissions before using another person’s footage, text, likeness or other protected material. A reference is inspiration, not automatic reuse permission.

Review your final script, captions and actual product view together. Have an unfamiliar person describe the promise and the demonstrated action. If they do not match, revise before sharing. Observing a popular reference does not guarantee the same results for your version.

sections.heading: Define the question and hold the offer steady
paragraphs: A format test compares two or more ways to communicate a similar message. Write a narrow question such as “Can viewers understand this feature more clearly in a reaction-plus-demo or a text-led video?” Keep the product fact, audience and intended next action as comparable as practical. If you change the offer, audience and message at the same time, a difference in results cannot be attributed to format alone.
This is a planning example, not a completed experiment. The fictional feature is a project call note with a next-step section.

sections.heading: Create the two concepts
paragraphs: Version A: a short reaction hook says “the next step is right here,” followed by a real recording that opens the note and shows its section. Version B: a wall-of-text overlay describes the same task and supported feature over appropriate footage. Each version should communicate the action accurately and use assets you have permission to publish.

Keep a simple record of exact wording, duration, account, destination and dates. The versions do not need identical editing, but differences that matter should be documented. Do not call these drafts completed or claim a winner before actual evidence exists.

sections.heading: Decide what you will observe
paragraphs: Before publishing, select a primary question and the platform’s available measure. For comprehension, a small review with unfamiliar viewers can ask what the app does after one viewing. For platform performance, record the platform-defined views and available retention or engagement metrics, together with the audience and distribution context. Metric definitions vary, and views do not equal customers or revenue.

Avoid setting an arbitrary universal threshold. Decide in advance what evidence would justify another iteration, and record sample size. Organic distribution, timing and unequal audiences can make comparisons noisy.

sections.heading: Interpret and iterate cautiously
paragraphs: After the agreed observation window, record both results and the conditions. If data is sparse or one format reached a different audience, describe the outcome as inconclusive rather than declaring a winner. If reviewers misunderstand the same feature in both versions, improve the explanation before testing another format.

Choose one next revision and keep the previous scripts and exports for comparison. Do not invent numbers or assume a format that worked for another account will work for yours. Secure any permissions and approvals before actual publication.

sections.heading: Build a five-slide feature story
paragraphs: Slide 1: “The call is over. The follow-up is tomorrow.” Slide 2: “You need to remember what the team agreed to do next.” Slide 3: “Keep the next-step section with the call note.” Slide 4: “Open the note when you are ready to follow up.” Slide 5: “Start from the next action.”

The story follows one situation through an actual feature. It does not claim automatic reminders, a measurable time saving, or a customer outcome. Replace the example with facts you can verify in your own app.

sections.heading: Assign a truthful visual to each slide
paragraphs: Use an owned or licensed visual for the setup, then a sanitized real screenshot for the feature when available. A generated picture of an interface can illustrate an idea, but should not be labeled as a real product screen. Keep enough context around the feature for the viewer to understand where it lives.
If you do not yet have permission to show a screen or customer data, prepare the slide copy and visual brief first. Obtain the right asset before publishing a visual that implies a real product view.

sections.heading: Review for story, accuracy and readability
paragraphs: Read the slides in order. The opening should promise the same situation the later slides address, and each slide should add a new part of the story. If readers need exact clicks or setup instructions, link to a tutorial rather than squeezing unsupported directions into a feature overview.
Preview the export at phone size, checking contrast, cropped controls and the destination named at the end. This is a planning example; it does not promise views or conversion.

title: Write a first slide that gives the rest of the carousel a clear job
description: Write an opening slide that promises the same useful SaaS story or tutorial the rest of your slideshow delivers.
lede: Write an opening slide that promises the same useful SaaS story or tutorial the rest of your slideshow delivers.
intent: Several full carousel openings paired with the body they promise

sections.heading: Make the opening a promise to the reader
paragraphs: An opening slide should help the intended reader decide whether the remaining slides address their task. Write the body first, then describe its actual subject in one short line. A curiosity gap can invite a swipe, but it should not promise a result or feature the later slides do not show.
The examples below use a fictional notes app with a call note and a next-step section. They are original planning examples, not recorded campaigns or verified outcomes.

sections.heading: Pair each opening with its body
paragraphs: For a story sequence about finding an agreed action after a call, an opening could be “the call is over. where did the next step go?” The body should then show the situation, the note, and the next-step section. It should not turn into an unrelated list of generic productivity tips.

For a tutorial sequence, “how to find the next step from a call” sets an instructional expectation. Follow it with the project, call note, next-step section and a review step. Confirm the real interface before using those instructions.
For a feature story, “keep the next step with the call note” names the feature directly. The following slides should explain its context and show the actual section where permitted.

sections.heading: Remove unsupported hooks
paragraphs: “This app sends every follow-up for you” is a poor opening if the body only shows a note. Either demonstrate a verified sending feature and its conditions or replace the claim with the action that is actually visible. Avoid invented statistics, testimonials or promises of instant results.
Write a short promise check: opening claim, body slide that supports it, and source of evidence. If no body slide answers the promise, revise the opening or the sequence.

sections.heading: Review the first slide on a phone
paragraphs: Use readable text and enough contrast against an owned or permissioned visual. A long title may need fewer words instead of smaller type. Check that cropping or platform controls do not obscure the text. Then view all slides in order and ask a reader what the opening led them to expect and whether the sequence answered it.
Save the exact opening and body together so a later revision does not accidentally break the match. This is a clarity exercise, not a guarantee of higher reach.
