sections.heading: Give the first words a single job
paragraphs: The opening overlay should point toward the feature or task the next shot reveals. It is not a place to summarize every product benefit. Write the actual screen action first, then use a short line that prepares the viewer to understand it. The following examples are fictional creative plans for a note-taking SaaS product, not tested ads or customer quotes.
The assumed feature is a call note containing a next-step section. A real founder must replace this assumption with a feature the actual app can show.

sections.heading: Write and compare complete pairs
paragraphs: Pair A: opening words “wait, the next steps are right here” followed by a screen recording that opens the call note and reveals the next-step section. Pair B: “the call ended. now what?” followed by the same screen, with a brief label “open the call note.” The first names the discovery; the second introduces the task.

A mismatched pair says “my follow-up sends itself” over a recording that only shows a note. The text implies automation and sending that the screen does not prove. Replace it with a supported phrase or demonstrate the actual verified feature.

sections.heading: Keep the selected words unchanged through editing
paragraphs: Once the wording is approved, store it as exact text with its capitalization, punctuation and line breaks. Add it in an editable text layer, then compare the export against the approved version. Do not ask a video model to render precise words and assume spelling will be correct.
Place the overlay where it remains readable without hiding the presenter or product control. If a bridge label is needed, treat it as separate text rather than changing the meaning of the opening.

sections.heading: Review the promise and proof together
paragraphs: Watch the first two shots on a phone without pausing. Ask a reviewer what the opening promised and what the product actually showed. If the answers differ, adjust the words or record a clearer action. Remove personal claims or quantified outcomes unless the speaker and evidence support them.
Use sanitized product footage and permissioned assets. A short reaction may create curiosity, but it does not guarantee views or make a fictional customer experience true.

title: End a SaaS slideshow with a useful next action
description: Write a SaaS slideshow ending that follows naturally from the preceding slides and leads to a relevant, accurate destination.
lede: Write a SaaS slideshow ending that follows naturally from the preceding slides and leads to a relevant, accurate destination.
intent: Complete ending-to-destination examples connected to full slide sequences

sections.heading: Start with what the body has delivered
paragraphs: An ending works when it completes the promise of the opening and gives the reader a relevant next action. First list what the slides actually teach or show. Then choose an ending that matches the reader’s likely next task. A generic “learn more” can be appropriate, but it should point to a page that really contains the promised information.
The examples below are fictional planning exercises. They do not describe real customers or measured results.

sections.heading: Complete a problem-solution story
paragraphs: Example sequence: slide 1, “the call is over. where did the next step go?” Slide 2, “you need the action the team agreed on.” Slide 3, “open the project call note.” Slide 4, “check the next-step section.” Slide 5, “start with the next step.” If a relevant feature page exists, the caption or link can say “See how project notes work” and lead there.

Do not send the reader to an unrelated signup page while promising a tutorial, and do not state that the product sends the follow-up unless it really does. The fictional notes feature must be replaced with verified product facts.

sections.heading: Complete a tutorial sequence
paragraphs: Example tutorial: slide 1, “how to find the next step from a call”; slide 2, “open the project”; slide 3, “choose the call note”; slide 4, “find the next-step section”; slide 5, “review the next action.” A useful ending might invite the reader to repeat the task in their own project, or open a verified product guide with the full instructions.
The story ending reinforces a situation; the tutorial ending reinforces a completed task. Both should be accurate for the real app and the current destination.

sections.heading: Check the destination and the final export
paragraphs: Open the proposed link yourself and make sure it resolves to the intended page, works on a phone and does not promise information absent from that page. If a destination requires signup or payment, do not imply immediate free access. Remove invented scarcity or deadlines.

Read the full sequence on a phone. Verify that the final text is legible, that any platform control does not hide it, and that the exact ending in the export matches the approved copy. A well-matched ending is a clarity improvement, not a guaranteed conversion tactic.

title: Adapt one presenter-led product explanation for different SaaS users
description: Write two distinct talking-head scripts for different SaaS audiences by changing the task and evidence, not just the audience name.
lede: Write two distinct talking-head scripts for different SaaS audiences by changing the task and evidence, not just the audience name.
intent: Two genuinely different audience tasks and full scripts, not swapped nouns

sections.heading: Separate the tasks before writing
paragraphs: Two audiences can use the same broad product category for different reasons. Write down the person, the moment and the job they need to do. Then choose a product action that can genuinely support that job. Changing “founder” to “manager” in the same script is not enough if the situation and proof remain identical.
The following fictional examples use a notes product with project call notes and next-step sections. They are planning exercises, not real customer stories.

sections.heading: Script one: preparing a follow-up
paragraphs: Audience: a founder preparing for a follow-up after a discovery call. Speaker: “After a call, check what you agreed to do next before you reply.” Show the project, the call note and its next-step section. Speaker: “Open the note and start with the action you recorded.” The relevant proof is the specific note and section.
If the real product does not include a next-step section, replace the task with a capability you can verify. Do not claim that it writes or sends the reply automatically.

sections.heading: Script two: handing context to a teammate
paragraphs: Audience: a teammate taking over an existing project. Speaker: “Taking over a project? Start by checking the notes from the last call.” Show the project and the relevant call note. Speaker: “Read the recorded next step before deciding what to do next.” The task is understanding handoff context, not preparing the original caller’s reply.

These scripts use related screens but a different moment, motivation and next action. If the product has no way to share a note with that teammate, do not imply sharing permissions or access; verify access before using the scenario.

sections.heading: Review both versions separately
paragraphs: For each script, match every factual statement to the actual interface and show only data that may be shared. Use a real speaker or an illustrative generated presenter without inventing a personal endorsement. Captions should match speech and stay clear of the control the viewer needs to see.

Ask one intended reader from each group, where available, to explain the task after watching. Record their feedback without fabricating a quote. Different audience fit is a hypothesis to review, not a claim that either version will perform better.

title: Give a presenter the voice of your SaaS without inventing a testimonial
description: Create a SaaS talking-head voice brief and rewrite one script in different tones while preserving truthful product facts.
lede: Create a SaaS talking-head voice brief and rewrite one script in different tones while preserving truthful product facts.
intent: Original voice brief and several reviewed spoken examples with claim boundaries

sections.heading: Describe voice as choices a speaker can follow
paragraphs: A useful voice brief specifies sentence length, vocabulary, level of energy and how directly to address the audience. Avoid vague instructions such as “sound viral.” Choose characteristics that fit your audience and the actual speaker. A calm, direct voice and an energetic voice can both be natural if the words are accurate and comfortable to say aloud.
This is a fictional writing exercise. The example app has project call notes with a next-step section; it is not a customer story or a recorded performance.

sections.heading: Start with a shared factual script
paragraphs: Neutral draft: “After a call, open the project note and check the next-step section. Use that to decide what to do next.” The only product fact is the location of the section. Verify that feature and its labels in your own app. If the section needs manual entry, avoid implying that it appears automatically.

A concise, practical version: “Call finished? Open the note and check the next step.” A warmer version: “When the call wraps up, open your project note. Your next-step section gives you somewhere to start.” Both express the same assumed behavior without making a time-saving claim.

sections.heading: Set boundaries for the speaker
paragraphs: Example brief: use short everyday sentences; speak to one viewer; use a relaxed pace; avoid exaggerated promises; show the product action as it is named. Add words your brand genuinely uses and remove phrases your speaker would not naturally say. Review any generated presenter so it does not appear to give a real customer endorsement.

Do not write “I use this every day” or “this saved me hours” for a speaker unless the experience is true and substantiated. A fictional persona can communicate a product explanation without claiming a personal result.

sections.heading: Review delivery against the screen
paragraphs: Read the script aloud and compare each spoken line with the actual product recording. Check captions against the approved transcript and move them if they obscure the important control. Ask a reviewer whether the tone fits the brand and whether the viewer can identify the task.
Record the approved words and observations from an actual review before calling a version tested. The writing examples here do not establish a better-performing voice.

title: Choose a spoken explanation or a silent reaction for an app feature

lede: Choose a silent reaction or spoken explanation for the same SaaS demo by comparing context, proof and editing effort.

sections.heading: Start with the same product task
paragraphs: A silent reaction can introduce a visual discovery; a talking-head explanation can give context the screen does not make obvious. Both still need a real product recording that demonstrates the promised action. Select the format after identifying what the audience needs to understand.
The fictional example is a notes app with a call note and next-step section. These are planning concepts, not recorded versions or performance results.

sections.heading: Plan a silent reaction version
paragraphs: Opening overlay: “wait, the next steps are right here.” Show a brief reaction, then cut to a sanitized recording opening the call note and revealing the section. The viewer needs to understand the task from the overlay and screen. If the initial product frame is unclear, add a short bridge label or show more context.
The reaction illustrates an emotion. It does not establish that a real customer discovered the feature or that the app automatically created the next steps.

sections.heading: Plan a spoken explanation version
paragraphs: Speaker: “After a call, open the project note and check the next-step section.” Show the project and the note while the instruction is spoken. Speaker: “That is where you can review the action you recorded.” Use the real interface labels and disclose any manual setup needed for the feature.

Speech gives the viewer more context but requires a clear transcript, delivery and captions that do not hide the control. It may be unnecessary if the action is obvious from the first screen and a brief overlay.

sections.heading: Choose with a comprehension review
paragraphs: Use the reaction plan when the feature is visible quickly and a short opening sets up the discovery. Use the explanation when the viewer needs a reason, condition or instruction before the screen makes sense. If neither version can demonstrate the claim, change the message or capture better proof.

Before publishing, record both actual versions only if you have permissioned assets and capacity, then ask viewers what action the app supports. A planning comparison cannot prove which format will earn more views or customers.

title: Choose hook, talking-head, wall text or slideshow from a reference idea
description: Choose between reaction-plus-demo, wall-of-text and slideshow treatments for the same SaaS message.
lede: Choose between reaction-plus-demo, wall-of-text and slideshow treatments for the same SaaS message.
intent: Same business brief expressed in distinct full formats with choice rationale

sections.heading: Extract the task before selecting a reference format
paragraphs: A reference can suggest a format, but the format should serve your viewer’s task and your actual product. Identify the verified feature, the proof available and whether the reader needs to see a screen action, read a short story or follow several steps. Record the reference source and use only assets you have permission to reuse.
The examples below are fictional plans for NorthStar Notes, a notes app with a call note and next-step section. They are not finished assets or measured results.

sections.heading: Express the same brief three ways
paragraphs: Reaction plus demo: “wait, the next steps are right here,” followed by a real recording that opens the note and holds the section. Choose this when the feature can be understood visually in a short sequence.

Wall of text: “the call is over. the follow-up is tomorrow. open the project note and check the next-step section.” Place the words over calm permissioned footage. Choose this when the situation and written observation are the main message.

Slideshow: “where did the next step go?” then the post-call situation, open the project note, check the section, and start with the next action. Choose this when the reader benefits from separate beats or instructions.

sections.heading: Match proof and production constraints
paragraphs: A generated background illustrates a scene; it does not demonstrate your software. Use an actual sanitized screen recording or screenshot when the message depends on showing the interface. Confirm labels, access conditions and whether the user must create the note manually. If a reference depends on a feature you do not have, change the claim rather than copying it.
Use original text and footage or obtain the appropriate permission for each reused element. A popular reference does not establish permission or guarantee that your version will have similar results.

sections.heading: Make a decision and review it
paragraphs: Choose the format that most directly explains the task with the proof you can supply. If all three contain the same words and no distinct purpose, develop one useful asset rather than making near-duplicates. Preview the final version on a phone and ask an unfamiliar viewer to identify the product action.
Record the chosen concept and the actual review feedback. Treat audience fit and performance as hypotheses until you observe real data.

sections.heading: Start with the promised task

A video, wall-of-text clip and carousel can make the same claim in different ways; each still needs accurate facts and appropriate permissions.
The examples in this guide are fictional review scenarios. They are not actual corrected exports, customer feedback or campaign outcomes.

sections.heading: Review a hook plus demo
paragraphs: Fictional draft opening: “my follow-up sends itself.” The visible screen only contains a call note. Flag the mismatch: the note alone does not demonstrate automatic sending. A proposed correction is “the next step is in the call note,” followed by the actual section, if the product supports it. Save a real corrected export and reviewer notes before calling the issue fixed.
Check that the reaction footage may be used, private data is removed and the product is readable at phone size.

sections.heading: Review a wall-of-text video or slideshow

A generated scene can illustrate context but does not prove customer use. For a slideshow, verify that the opening matches the body, each slide advances the task, any screen is genuine and sanitized, and the final destination delivers what the ending promises.
Flag unsupported claims such as invented savings, guaranteed outcomes or a testimonial the speaker did not provide. Remove or substantiate them before sharing.

title: Make the transition from reaction footage to app proof understandable
description: Plan a clear cut from an AI reaction hook to real product footage, with three transition options and a practical timing worksheet.
lede: Plan a clear cut from an AI reaction hook to real product footage, with three transition options and a practical timing worksheet.
intent: Actual hard-cut, bridge-label and held-result variants of one owned sequence

sections.heading: Pick the frame the viewer needs to understand
paragraphs: The transition is the moment between the reaction and the product proof. It can be a direct cut, a short label, or a brief view of the result before the interaction. The best choice depends on whether the first product frame makes sense without narration. Record the app with a shareable account and identify the earliest frame that shows where the action begins.
For this fictional example, a creator reacts to finding next steps in a call note. The real demo you make would show your own app. No recorded result or performance is implied by this plan.

sections.heading: Choose one of three transitions
paragraphs: A hard cut is suitable when the opening and first app frame already share context: “the next step is right here,” followed by a readable note. Trim dead time before the note appears, but keep enough of the interface to understand what was opened.

A bridge label helps when the app view otherwise arrives without context. Use a brief instruction such as “open the call note,” then show that action. A held-result opening starts with the next-step section before showing how to reach it; use it only when the held frame is genuine footage of the actual product state.

sections.heading: Check the handoff at normal speed
paragraphs: On a timeline, label the last reaction frame, the first product frame and the frame where the promised feature is legible. Play the cut without pausing. If the viewer cannot tell what changed, allow a little context or use a bridge label. If the product takes too long to appear, remove an unrelated intermediate screen rather than speeding through information people need.

Captions and the app interface can compete for the same space. Move or shorten a caption if it hides the feature; review the exported video on a phone, not just in a large editor preview. Keep original overlay words editable and check them separately from generated footage.

sections.heading: Choose the transition by clarity
paragraphs: Ask a second person what they expected to see after the reaction and where the feature appeared. A direct cut is simpler only when they can follow it. If all three variants still need an explanation, re-record a clearer starting frame or simplify the hook. A single concrete action is easier to understand than an entire product tour.

This example is a fictional planning brief for NorthStar Notes: a project call note contains a next-step section. It is not a customer story or an actual export.

sections.heading: Write the complete script and shot plan
paragraphs: Speaker: “After a call, you might need to find the next step before following up.” Cut to a project recording. Speaker: “Open the project and choose the call note.” Show that action. Speaker: “The next-step section is in the note, so you can check what comes next.” Hold the section long enough to read it.

sections.heading: Keep the handoff understandable

If a transition feels abrupt, a short bridge label can clarify where the viewer is. Time speech with the visible action; do not say “here” while the relevant control is hidden.

title: Keep track of source inspiration, permissions and your final creative
description: Record where a creative reference came from, what you may reuse and what must be created independently before making a SaaS video.
lede: Record where a creative reference came from, what you may reuse and what must be created independently before making a SaaS video.
intent: Practical provenance record with owned worked example; no rights guarantee

sections.heading: Record the source before you remix
paragraphs: A reference can inform pacing, story structure or presentation, but it may also contain another person’s footage, words, music or likeness. Record where you found it and who owns the components before making a reuse decision. A public link or the ability to view an asset does not by itself establish permission to copy it.
This guide offers an operational checklist, not a legal determination. Licensing terms and permissions vary. When rights are unclear, use original or appropriately licensed material or seek advice.

sections.heading: Create a practical provenance record
paragraphs: For each reference, record its source URL, creator or account if known, date accessed, elements you want to use, the permission or license and its limits, and where that evidence is stored. Separate the license for video from any music, spoken words or on-screen text if they have different owners. Do not record private customer details in a public brief.

For an illustrative fictional example, a founder notes that a public video uses a surprised opening and a product reveal. The founder records the link for research, writes a new script based on their own verified feature, and uses their own footage. No claim is made that the original video is licensed for reuse.

sections.heading: Decide what to create independently
paragraphs: Describe an idea in functional terms such as “reaction followed by screen proof.” Write original words rather than copying a creator’s full overlay. Use an owned presenter or a properly licensed asset, and create your own product recording. If a particular video, quote, sound or likeness is essential, check the specific authorization and scope before using it.
If permission is denied, unavailable or limited to a different channel, remove that element or request suitable permission. Do not assume credit alone replaces permission.

sections.heading: Recheck the final asset
paragraphs: Match the finished export against the record: every third-party element should have a source and permission that covers the intended use. title: Write different hook-plus-demo edits for problem-aware and product-aware viewers
description: Plan two hook-plus-demo briefs for people who recognize a problem and people who already know the product, without claiming either edit has been tested.
lede: Plan two hook-plus-demo briefs for people who recognize a problem and people who already know the product, without claiming either edit has been tested.
intent: Distinct complete briefs and reviewed cuts for the two viewer states

sections.heading: Identify what the viewer already knows
paragraphs: A problem-aware viewer recognizes a task or frustration but may not know your product. A product-aware viewer already knows the product and may be looking for a specific feature. These are planning assumptions, not fixed labels for every individual. Use them to decide how much context the first shot needs.
For the fictional examples below, NorthStar Notes has a project call note with a next-step section. The examples are scripts and shot plans, not customer data or reviewed cuts.

sections.heading: Brief A: lead with the task
paragraphs: Audience assumption: someone who has just finished a call and needs to find the agreed next action. Opening overlay: “the call ended. where did the next step go?” A short reaction introduces the uncertainty. Then show a real, sanitized product recording opening the project note and revealing its next-step section. End with “check the next step before the follow-up.”

The message does not assume the audience knows the product name or interface. It also does not claim the app writes or sends the follow-up. If the actual app cannot show the assumed section, choose a different feature and rewrite the entire brief.

sections.heading: Brief B: lead with the known feature
paragraphs: Audience assumption: an existing user who knows the app but has not noticed the next-step section. Opening: “the next steps are in the call note.” Show the project, open the note and hold the relevant section. End with “open the call note to find it.” This version can name the interface earlier because the assumed viewer already has context.
Verify the real screen labels and any access conditions. Do not imply that every user already has content in the section; it may require manual input.

sections.heading: Review the two versions as separate briefs
paragraphs: Compare the opening, first screen and closing action. If both versions need the same explanation and show the same task, combine them instead of creating two nearly identical assets. Before publishing, record the actual screens and test whether representative viewers can explain the relevant action. Preserve only observations you really collect.
Use permissioned footage and accurate captions. Neither audience assumption predicts retention or conversions; any performance comparison requires a real, carefully interpreted test.

title: Hand off from spoken explanation to a visible software action
description: Plan a clear handoff between a talking-head explanation and a real software demonstration, with an editable timing worksheet.
lede: Plan a clear handoff between a talking-head explanation and a real software demonstration, with an editable timing worksheet.
intent: Timestamped narration/control/result examples and corrected transitions

sections.heading: Mark the sentence and action that must meet
paragraphs: A speech-to-demo handoff is clear when the viewer sees the relevant control or result as the speaker describes it. Write the script and identify the exact product action first. Then choose the shot that shows the action with enough interface context. Avoid relying on a timestamp until you have the actual recording and can inspect it.
This fictional example uses a project call note with a next-step section. The timing below is an illustrative edit plan, not a measured clip or approved export.

sections.heading: Create a provisional timeline
paragraphs: For a short video, you might plan 0–3 seconds for the speaker saying “After a call, find the next step in the project note.” Around 3–6 seconds, the speaker says “Open the project and choose the call note” as the recording shows those actions. From 6 seconds onward, hold the next-step section while the speaker says “Check the action you recorded.” These are flexible planning ranges, not universal duration rules.

Once you have the actual clips, mark the frame where the control becomes visible and the frame where the result is readable. Adjust the speech, trim or hold rather than assuming the provisional timing fits.

sections.heading: Fix common timing problems
paragraphs: If the spoken instruction begins before the interface appears, add a brief lead-in or move the cut earlier. If the screen action is too fast, hold a readable frame or re-record at a comfortable pace. If the control is hidden by captions, reposition or shorten the captions while preserving the approved spoken words.
Do not crop so tightly that the viewer loses the context needed to understand where the control is. Use a sanitized account and omit sensitive names, messages or other private information.

sections.heading: Check the export without narration assistance
paragraphs: Watch once at normal speed on a phone. Ask a reviewer what action was demonstrated and where the result appeared. If they cannot tell, revise the cut or capture a clearer screen. Compare captions and spoken words against the approved transcript, including any qualifiers or setup conditions.
The actual timestamps, screenshots and review findings must come from your own recording. This plan does not claim a video has been created or that a particular timing will perform better.

sections.heading: Identify what must remain visible
paragraphs: A talking-head demo can contain subtitles, product labels, a cursor and platform interface elements in the same vertical frame. A conflict occurs when captions cover the control or result being discussed, or when their timing or words disagree with speech. Start with the exact transcript and the actual recording.
The following is a fictional planning scenario: the speaker explains a next-step section in a call note. No actual overlapping or corrected export is claimed.

sections.heading: Map the collision over time
paragraphs: Mark the interval where the product control first appears and where it remains readable. Note the caption box, cursor and any overlays over that interval. A caption may be clear at the first frame but cover the result after a crop or pan. Review the full motion, not a single still.

In the example, the line “check the next-step section” appears across the bottom while the section is also at the bottom. A correction could move the caption to a clear upper region or reframe the screen with enough context. The actual choice depends on the recording.

sections.heading: Preserve speech while changing layout
paragraphs: Keep the words accurate; moving a caption is not permission to change the speaker’s meaning. Split a long caption at a natural phrase if both parts still match the timing and approved transcript. Check spelling, punctuation and any important conditions, such as a feature requiring manual setup.

If there is no safe place for both caption and product detail, briefly hold the screen, reduce unrelated content, or revise and re-record the script. Do not shrink the interface or captions until they become unreadable.

sections.heading: Review the exported result
paragraphs: Compare the final export to the approved words and watch it on a phone with sound on and off. Confirm that the control can be seen when the corresponding words appear and that the viewer can read the caption. Keep an actual before-and-after export only when you have permission to retain and share it.
Ask a reviewer to identify the spoken action and visible result. Record their real observation rather than claiming a correction has been tested before it exists.

sections.heading: Give the footage a supporting role
paragraphs: In a wall-of-text video, the words normally carry the main message. Choose footage that fits the situation without forcing the viewer to decode a second story at the same time. Before selecting a clip, write the approved overlay and identify the moment it describes.
This example is a fictional plan about finding next steps after a call. It does not describe an actual recorded clip or a measured creative result.

sections.heading: Compare a matched and a distracting plan
paragraphs: Overlay: “the call is over. the follow-up is tomorrow. open the project note and check the next-step section.” A calm desk or post-call moment could support that situation if you own or can license it, and if a clear area remains for text. A rapidly moving interface or a busy unrelated party scene would compete with the words and may make the message harder to follow.
If the message needs proof that a feature exists, include a real sanitized product screen where appropriate. A generated desk scene can illustrate context but cannot verify the software feature.

sections.heading: Check the entire moving frame
paragraphs: Preview the text over the whole clip at the intended phone size. Watch for moving hands, bright lights, faces or signage crossing the text. Check contrast in both bright and dark frames and ensure platform controls will not cover critical words. Adjust placement, add a suitable backing treatment or select a calmer clip rather than assuming the first frame represents the whole video.
Add the exact copy as editable text. Do not rely on generated pixels to reproduce the approved wording accurately.

sections.heading: Review rights and the final export
paragraphs: Record the source and permission for the background, music and any recognizable person. A reference link does not itself grant reuse rights. If permissions are unclear, select owned or appropriately licensed material. Avoid presenting an illustrative generated scene as a customer testimonial.

Watch the exported video at normal speed and ask someone to summarize the written message. If they cannot read it comfortably, shorten the copy or give it more time. Keep actual before-and-after clips and observations only when they have been created and approved.

sections.heading: Assign each slide a visual purpose
paragraphs: A visual brief tells a designer or editor what each slide needs to show and which asset may be used. Start with the approved slide copy and reader task, then identify the visual evidence needed. Do not make an invented interface look like an actual product screenshot.

The following is a fictional planning exercise for a notes product with a project call note and a next-step section. The asset descriptions are instructions, not a claim that approved assets already exist.

sections.heading: Build a five-slide brief
paragraphs: Slide 1, “where did the next step go?”: use an owned or licensed post-call visual with clear space for the words. Slide 2, “find the action you agreed on”: show an illustrative work moment, avoiding private messages. Slide 3, “open the project note”: use an actual sanitized product screenshot if permissioned.

Slide 4, “check the next-step section”: show the real section clearly, retaining enough surrounding interface for context. Slide 5, “start with the next action”: use a simple visual and an accurate destination. Replace these assumed screens with your own verified feature and interface.

sections.heading: Specify crop, hierarchy and rights
paragraphs: For every slide, record the asset source, permitted use, intended crop, main text and one focal point. Check whether screen labels remain legible at phone size. If a screenshot contains customer names or confidential information, use a sample account or remove the content before capture.

An AI-generated illustration may support a mood, but it must not be represented as proof that the app contains a particular interface or customer result. Obtain the appropriate permissions for any third-party image, font, icon or identifiable person.

sections.heading: Approve the actual asset before export
paragraphs: Compare each finished slide against the brief. Verify the copy and product facts, the source of each visual, the legibility of the interface and the destination on the final slide. If the approved asset is not available, mark the slide as incomplete instead of substituting an unsupported screenshot.
Review the actual exported sequence in order on a phone. The brief is a plan; it does not establish that screenshots were captured, rights secured or the creative tested.

title: Keep visual continuity between a creator reaction and the product demo
description: Plan visual continuity between a reaction clip and a SaaS screen recording using eyeline, movement and orientation checks.
lede: Plan visual continuity between a reaction clip and a SaaS screen recording using eyeline, movement and orientation checks.
intent: Annotated eyeline, motion and orientation examples from owned clips

sections.heading: Decide what continuity needs to do
paragraphs: Visual continuity helps a viewer understand that the opening and product view belong to the same idea. It does not require pretending that a generated creator actually used the app. Start with the approved hook and the product action that proves it; visual matching cannot fix an unsupported claim.
The examples below are fictional shot plans. They are not annotated frames from an owned recording or proof that an edit has been made.

sections.heading: Plan eyeline and transition
paragraphs: If the creator looks to the right and the next shot shows an app screen, a simple cut may feel coherent when the screen appears in a consistent direction. Alternatively, use a neutral forward-facing reaction and a clear screen cut. Do not force an eyeline that hides the face or makes the action unnatural.

Write down the last visible reaction frame and first product frame after you actually obtain the footage. Check whether the viewer can tell what changed. If the connection is unclear, add a short truthful bridge label rather than implying a real interaction that did not occur.

sections.heading: Review movement and orientation
paragraphs: A moving hand or camera can make a cut feel abrupt if the screen suddenly moves in a conflicting direction. Consider a still product frame or a short pause when the motion is distracting. For vertical social video, confirm that the app screen is readable within the portrait frame and preserve enough interface context around the feature.
Do not stretch or crop the product view until controls are unrecognizable. If a screen requires a landscape capture, plan the crop and show only a genuine, sanitized view.

sections.heading: Annotate actual frames before approval
paragraphs: Capture the real end frame of the hook, the first demo frame and the result frame from assets you may use. Note the eyeline, direction of movement and readable feature in each; compare them at phone size. Ask an unfamiliar reviewer what action the edit shows.

Do not label a planning diagram as a real before-and-after example. Secure rights for any third-party footage and verify captions and product facts in the final export. No performance result can be inferred from this plan.

sections.heading: Start with the source dimensions
paragraphs: A portrait reaction clip and a widescreen product recording have different shapes. Before editing, note each source’s dimensions, the target canvas and the part of the interface that must remain legible. Avoid assuming a single crop will work for every app. The examples here are planning instructions, not actual source or exported frame comparisons.
The product recording should use an account and data you may share. A generated reaction can illustrate a mood but does not establish real customer use.

sections.heading: Choose how the wide screen enters the vertical frame
paragraphs: Fit the whole screen when the surrounding context is necessary, but check whether the control is still readable. Crop toward the relevant region when it remains possible to understand where the action occurs. Another option is to show a wider establishing view first and then cut to a closer, genuine view of the control.

Do not stretch the recording or remove conditions that change the meaning of the action. If the necessary information remains too small, re-record a closer view or split the explanation into separate scenes.

sections.heading: Preserve a clean reaction shot
paragraphs: Keep the reaction’s face and intended performance visible within the target frame. Check that captions and platform interface elements do not hide the face or important app controls. A reaction should lead to a specific supported product claim; it does not need to appear simultaneously with the entire screen.

If using a picture-in-picture layout, check both elements at actual phone size. When the app becomes too small to understand, use sequential full-frame shots instead of forcing the pair into one view.

sections.heading: Compare the actual source and export
paragraphs: Save representative source frames and corresponding final frames from permissioned footage. Note what was cropped, whether the feature is legible and whether the viewer retains enough orientation. Watch the complete export on a phone and verify approved text and sensitive-data removal.

title: When should the result appear before the reaction in a SaaS video?
description: Choose whether a SaaS video should show the product result before a reaction or introduce the reaction first.
lede: Choose whether a SaaS video should show the product result before a reaction or introduce the reaction first.
intent: Owned result-first versus reaction-first edits, tradeoffs and comprehension notes

sections.heading: Define the result and what proves it
paragraphs: Result-first starts with a visible product state, then explains how it was reached. Reaction-first begins with a creator or text reacting to a feature, followed by the product view. In either case the result must be real, understandable and supported by the app. A result cannot be an invented customer outcome or a generated screenshot presented as evidence.
This fictional planning example uses a call note with a next-step section. It does not describe an actual edited video or an experiment.

sections.heading: Plan a result-first sequence
paragraphs: Show the sanitized note and its next-step section. Overlay: “the next step is in the call note.” Then show a reaction and the steps used to open the note. The first frame gives a concrete answer, but it must remain legible and the following shots should explain how to reach it. If the result requires a user to enter information, do not suggest the app created it automatically.
Use result-first when the screen can be understood quickly and the viewer benefits from seeing the destination before the navigation.

sections.heading: Plan a reaction-first sequence
paragraphs: Open with the exact words “wait, the next steps are right here” and a brief reaction. Cut to the project, open the note and hold the section. This can set up curiosity, but it needs to show the promised feature promptly and accurately. If the first product screen lacks context, add a concise bridge or change the starting frame.

Keep the task, underlying claim and next action consistent between the plans if you later compare them. Do not change several other variables and claim that the opening order alone caused a difference.

sections.heading: Review the real versions before drawing conclusions
paragraphs: If you make both versions, record the actual assets, export dates, captions and distribution conditions. Ask viewers what the product does after one viewing and document real feedback. Platform distribution and audience differences can affect metrics, so small or unequal samples may be inconclusive.
If you do not have both approved clips, treat the comparison as a decision guide. It is not a claim that either version has been tested or is guaranteed to perform better.

sections.heading: Choose one feature with multiple real uses
paragraphs: A series is useful when each episode answers a different question, not when the same clip is republished with a changed adjective. Start with one feature you can verify, then list separate audience tasks that it actually supports. Plan each opening, screen action and ending together.
These three episodes are fictional planning exercises for a note-taking app with project call notes and a next-step section. They are not owned videos or customer results.

sections.heading: Episode 1: find the next step after a call
paragraphs: Opening: “the call ended. where did the next step go?” Product proof: open the relevant project and call note, then show its next-step section. Ending: “check the action you recorded.” This episode addresses the caller preparing to follow up. Do not claim automatic writing or sending unless the real product demonstrates it.
Record a sanitized note that the viewer can read, and confirm the section actually exists in the current interface.

sections.heading: Episode 2 and 3: two different contexts
paragraphs: Episode 2, teammate handoff: “taking over this project? start with the last call note.” Show the project and a note the teammate is authorized to access. End with “review the recorded next action.” Verify that the teammate can actually access the note before claiming a handoff.

Episode 3, preparing for a later meeting: “before the next meeting, check what was agreed last time.” Show the prior call note and its next-step section. End with “bring the recorded action into the next discussion.” This is a preparation context, not a claim that the product automatically schedules a meeting.

sections.heading: Review each episode on its own
paragraphs: Make an evidence record for each actual clip: approved hook words, product screen, permission, export and review feedback. If two episodes show the same task and proof with no meaningful distinction, combine them. If a proposed episode depends on a feature or permission you lack, revise or leave it unproduced.
Watch each final export at phone size and check exact overlays. These briefs do not establish that the episodes have been filmed, reviewed or tested.

sections.heading: Record the asset before evaluating it
paragraphs: An iteration log links a specific creative revision to the observation that prompted it. Record the asset name, version, format, product claim, approved source and destination. Store a link to an actual export if one exists, and note whether it is approved for internal or external use. Avoid copying private account data into the log.
The entries in this guide are fictional examples of how to structure a record. They are not actual review notes, user interviews or campaign results.

sections.heading: Separate the observation from the change
paragraphs: For a fictional demo, a review note could be recorded as: “Observation to verify: a reviewer could not identify the next-step section on the phone preview.” The proposed revision is “hold the section longer and move the caption away from the control.” The evidence field should link to the actual reviewed clip and feedback once those exist. Until then, label the entry a planning example.
Do not write “viewers preferred version B” unless a real review produced that conclusion. Do not invent watch time, conversions or a user quotation to make a decision appear conclusive.

sections.heading: Make the next test specific
paragraphs: Record one change you intend to evaluate: for example, keep the same supported feature and compare a longer screen hold with the earlier cut. Record the intended audience, platform, observation period and metric definition. If the audience or offer also changes, note that a difference cannot be attributed solely to the screen hold.
For pre-publication comprehension, ask a reviewer to describe the feature and action. Save the actual response with permission rather than turning an imagined response into evidence.

sections.heading: Close the loop after a real review
paragraphs: Add the new export version and record what was actually observed. If sample size is small or conditions differ, write “inconclusive” and choose a sensible next step. Check that the product still supports every claim and that footage and screen data may be shared.
Retain the previous version and date so a team member can understand what changed. This log supports careful decisions; it does not guarantee improved reach or conversion.

sections.heading: Understand the reference before adapting
paragraphs: Record the source and the role of each segment: opening, context, proof and ending. Separate a creative structure from the reference creator’s words, footage, music, identity and product claims. A public reference does not automatically provide permission to reuse any of its assets.

sections.heading: Build from your own verified facts
paragraphs: Write the intended viewer task, your actual feature and the product action a recording can show. For a fictional notes app, the supported planning fact could be that a call note contains a next-step section. A reference about automatically sending follow-ups cannot be copied into this product concept unless that feature genuinely exists.

sections.heading: Write an original adaptation
paragraphs: A hypothetical new sequence might be “wait, the next step is right here,” followed by an independently recorded note and a readable section. Write original words, use your own footage or properly licensed assets, and verify any conditions. This is a concept plan, not an analysis of a specific permissioned reference or a finished asset.

sections.heading: Document the real transformation
paragraphs: Before treating the article as an example, provide a permissioned source, a source analysis, a verified product brief and an approved original final asset. Check exact copy, private data and rights. Do not promise that your adaptation will reproduce another creator’s results.

title: Choose a reference emotion that fits the product message

intent: Several supported emotion/message pairings and owned outputs

sections.heading: Choose an emotion that fits the message
paragraphs: A reference may use surprise, curiosity, frustration or calm explanation. Decide what role the emotion plays in the opening and whether it fits the intended viewer’s task. The emotion is a creative choice; it is not proof that a customer experienced it.

sections.heading: Plan three supported pairings
paragraphs: For a fictional note feature: surprise, “wait, the next steps are in the note”; curiosity, “where did the next action go?”; calm explanation, “open the call note to check the next action.” Each needs the actual screen showing the supported feature. These are draft pairings, not recorded outputs or measured winners.

sections.heading: Avoid misleading performance
paragraphs: Do not make a generated presenter imply a genuine personal discovery or testimonial. Avoid exaggerated emotions that suggest the app did something it cannot do. Match the exact overlay and the next screen, and preserve any conditions such as manual entry.

sections.heading: Review actual variants
paragraphs: If creating multiple versions, keep the task and product proof consistent and document the genuine differences in expression. Record the actual assets, permission and feedback before describing a review. Different audiences and distribution conditions prevent a simple attribution of results to emotion alone.

sections.heading: Inventory inputs and rights
paragraphs: Record the reference source, the element you want to study and the rights covering any material you intend to reuse. Separate source wording from your own product facts. A source transcript is not evidence that your app has the same features or that its claims apply to your business.

sections.heading: Create a verified fact sheet
paragraphs: List the intended user, a specific task, the real feature, any conditions and the evidence source. For a fictional notes app, the example fact is “a project call note contains a next-step section.” This is a hypothetical brief, not an actual business profile or customer claim.

sections.heading: Remix the message, not the unsupported claim
paragraphs: If a reference says “the app sends the follow-up automatically” but the verified feature only displays a note, replace that claim with original words such as “open the note and check the next step.” Use the actual interface labels and do not add savings, integrations or automatic actions that are not supported.

sections.heading: Approve and preserve the output
paragraphs: Store the real source, rights, verified input facts, exact approved output and final asset together. Check that the wording remains unchanged through editing and that any screen recording is sanitized. Until actual inputs and approved output exist, describe this as a planning method rather than a completed remix.

title: Turn one SaaS feature into hook-demo, talking-head and wall-text videos
description: Plan the same verified SaaS feature as a reaction demo, a talking-head demo and a wall-of-text video.
lede: Plan the same verified SaaS feature as a reaction demo, a talking-head demo and a wall-of-text video.
intent: Three complete original assets using the same verified feature facts

sections.heading: Choose one feature and one audience task
paragraphs: A format comparison is useful when each version explains the same verified product behavior in a distinct way. Start with a real feature, its conditions and the proof you can show. The example below is a fictional plan for a call note with a next-step section, not three finished assets.

sections.heading: Plan a reaction plus demo
paragraphs: Opening text: “wait, the next steps are right here.” Follow with a real recording that opens the project note and holds the next-step section. End with the action “check the next step.” This format relies on a clear visible product reveal.

sections.heading: Plan a talking-head demo and a wall-of-text video
paragraphs: Talking-head script: “After a call, open the project note and check the next-step section.” Show the real navigation as the speaker names it, then hold the section long enough to read. Verify the real interface and do not imply the app created or sent a follow-up.

Wall-of-text overlay: “the call is over. the follow-up is tomorrow. open the project note and check the next step.” Pair the exact words with calm permissioned footage. The spoken version explains while showing the app; the text-led version carries the situation in written copy.

sections.heading: Compare completed assets carefully
paragraphs: Create each asset only with accurate facts, approved footage and readable text. Keep the same product promise and intended action if comparing formats, and record actual audience, timing and platform metrics. Do not call these plans actual assets or declare a winner without real evidence.

sections.heading: Hold the product message constant
paragraphs: A useful emotion comparison changes the performance while keeping the opening words, product feature and proof consistent. Pick one supported claim and a real app action. An AI presenter can illustrate a reaction but must not impersonate a real customer or assert an invented experience.

sections.heading: Write three performance directions
paragraphs: For the fictional line “the next steps are right here,” plan a restrained surprised reaction, a curious lean toward the screen and a calm look of recognition. In each version, follow with the same real note and next-step section. These are directions, not recorded clips or tested results.

sections.heading: Record the actual differences
paragraphs: Keep a version log with source, exact copy, visible action, timing and expression. Preserve the words exactly when comparing emotion; changing the claim or the screen at the same time makes the interpretation less clear. Use footage and people you have rights to use.

sections.heading: Review without inventing a winner
paragraphs: Ask an actual reviewer whether each opening feels natural and connects to the screen. Save real feedback and exports with permission. If later comparing platform results, document audience, timing and sample limits; a small or unequal sample cannot establish that an emotion caused a performance difference.

paragraphs: A useful breakdown identifies the exact hook, the first product frame and the visible action that answers the opening. Use a complete video you own or have permission to analyze and share. A list of hooks cannot show whether the later product view actually proves the opening.

sections.heading: Illustrative shot plan
paragraphs: For a fictional notes app, a planning sequence might be: reaction with “the next steps are right here”; a project screen; a call note opening; and a held view of a next-step section. sections.heading: Annotate an actual asset
paragraphs: For each shot record its start and end time, the exact text, the screen action and why it follows the previous shot. Capture a readable frame only when you have rights to reproduce it. Mark any unsupported claim or missing context and describe the actual revision, rather than presenting a hypothetical correction as a completed edit.

sections.heading: Review before publication
paragraphs: Check the final video for readable product proof, permissioned footage, accurate text and removed private data. Save the original asset, annotated frames and review notes. Do not claim that an example produced views or conversions without verified evidence.

sections.heading: Define the comparison honestly
paragraphs: A before-and-after comparison must identify the permissioned source and a demonstrably original output. “Before” should describe the source structure and claims accurately; “after” should show what was changed for the new product and why. Do not present a fictional reference as a real creator asset.

sections.heading: Use a hypothetical planning exercise
paragraphs: Imagine a source structure consisting of a surprised opening followed by an automatic-send demonstration. The fictional target product can only show a call note with next steps. A responsible proposed adaptation changes the words to “the next step is in the note” and shows an independently captured note. This is a conceptual example, not a completed before-and-after.

sections.heading: Capture the real evidence
paragraphs: Record the source link, creator and permission; annotate the relevant segment without copying unlicensed media. Save the target business facts and the independently created script and asset. Mark exactly which reference element informed the structure and which unsupported claims were removed.

sections.heading: Review rights and claims
paragraphs: Verify the output against the real feature, check permissions for footage and music, and remove private information. Include actual before-and-after assets and review notes only when approved. Do not imply that matching a popular format will reproduce its reach or sales.
